title: Improper Integrals
summary: Improper integrals have an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand. Replace the trouble with a limit: $\int_a^\infty f\,dx=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f\,dx$. If the limit is finite the integral converges; otherwise it diverges.

improper integral.plain: An integral with an infinite bound or a blowup.
improper integral.in_class: Defined by a limit of ordinary integrals.

converges.plain: The limit defining it is a finite number.
converges.in_class: The area is finite despite the infinite extent.

diverges.plain: The limit is infinite or does not exist.

type 2.in_class: A vertical asymptote inside or at an endpoint.

comparison test.plain: Bound your integrand by a known one.
comparison test.in_class: Smaller than a convergent ⇒ converges; bigger than a divergent ⇒ diverges.

split at the blowup.plain: Break the integral at an interior singularity.
split at the blowup.in_class: Each piece must converge on its own.

concept_sections.heading: Infinite intervals (Type 1)
concept_sections.explanation: Replace the infinite bound by $t$ and take a limit: $\int_a^\infty f\,dx=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f\,dx$. A finite limit means convergence.
math_steps: Rewrite with a finite upper limit $t$.

concept_sections.heading: Unbounded integrands (Type 2)
concept_sections.explanation: If $f$ blows up at an endpoint $c$, use $\lim_{t\to c}\int_a^t f\,dx$. If the blowup is interior, split there and require both halves to converge.
math_steps: Split at interior blowups; both pieces must converge.

concept_sections.heading: The $p$-test
concept_sections.explanation: The benchmark $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p>1$; $\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx$ converges when $p<1$. Memorize these thresholds.

concept_sections.heading: Comparison test
concept_sections.explanation: If $0\le f\le g$ and $\int g$ converges, so does $\int f$; if $f\ge g\ge0$ and $\int g$ diverges, so does $\int f$. Compare to a known $p$-integral.
math_steps: Bound $f$ above or below by a simpler $g$.

concept_sections.heading: Evaluating exactly
concept_sections.explanation: When it converges, compute the value: find the antiderivative, evaluate at $t$, and take the limit. Many give clean numbers like $1$ or $\ln$-free constants.

real_world_examples.title: Escape energy
real_world_examples.scenario: Work to move a rocket infinitely far from Earth.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Gravity $\propto1/r^2$ gives a convergent improper integral — finite escape energy.

real_world_examples.title: Probability tails
real_world_examples.scenario: A distribution stretching to infinity must total 1.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Normalizing a density requires a convergent improper integral over all outcomes.

real_world_examples.title: Steady-state accumulation
real_world_examples.scenario: A decaying signal integrated over all time.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Exponential decay $e^{-t}$ integrates to a finite total, converging.
